title: Can a table have more than one primary key (no: only one, but it can be composite)?
shortTitle: Can a table have more than one primary key?
keyPoints: A table can have at most one primary key, because the primary key is the single canonical identity of a row.
That one primary key can be composite – made of two or more columns whose combined values are unique.
A composite primary key is common in junction tables and weak entities that depend on a parent.
If you need several columns to be independently unique, add unique constraints, not additional primary keys.
Wide composite primary keys can hurt performance because they are copied into every secondary index and every foreign key reference.
Many teams prefer a single surrogate primary key and demote the natural composite to a unique constraint.

s1_definition.oneliner: Exactly one primary key per table, but it may be composite (several columns together); extra uniqueness needs unique constraints, not extra primary keys.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **One primary key** – a table can declare `PRIMARY KEY` only once, because the primary key is the single canonical identity of a row.
- **Composite primary key** – that one primary key can be made of two or more columns whose combined values are unique, even though no single column is unique on its own.
- **When to use composite** – junction tables (many-to-many), weak entities (detail rows that depend on a parent, like transaction line items).
- **Extra uniqueness** – if you need several columns to be independently unique, add `UNIQUE` constraints, not more primary keys.
- **Surrogate alternative** – many teams prefer a single narrow surrogate PK and demote the natural composite to a unique constraint for performance and ORM simplicity.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India gives each account exactly one official identity – there cannot be two "official" identities, or the ledger would not know which one is the truth. But that single official identity can be made of more than one piece. For a joint-holding record, the identity might be the pair of account number plus holder sequence, so neither alone is unique but together they are. That is still one primary key, just built from two columns.

```text
Single-column PK:           Composite PK:              Two PKs (INVALID):
┌─────────────────┐         ┌───────────────────────┐   ┌─────────────────┐
│ accounts        │         │ account_holders       │   │ accounts        │
├─────────────────┤         ├───────────────────────┤   ├─────────────────┤
│ account_id (PK) │         │ account_id ┐          │   │ account_id (PK) │
│ email (UNIQUE)  │         │ holder_seq ┘ (PK)     │   │ pan (PK)  ← ✗  │
│ pan (UNIQUE)    │         │ holder_name            │   │ ERROR!          │
│ balance         │         └───────────────────────┘   └─────────────────┘
└─────────────────┘              │
                           One PK, two columns
                           Combined uniqueness

Surrogate vs Composite PK:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Surrogate PK (BIGINT)       │ Composite PK (3 columns)       │
│ - 8 bytes in every index    │ - Up to 150 bytes in indexes  │
│ - Simple FK references      │ - Multi-column FK references  │
│ - Easy ORM mapping          │ - Requires @EmbeddedId in JPA │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
No, a table cannot have more than one primary key, and the reason is conceptual. The primary key is the single canonical identity of a row – the one handle the database and the rest of the system use to refer to it unambiguously. Two primary keys would mean two competing identities, and the database could not decide which one child tables reference or which one clusters the data.

What trips people up is the difference between more than one primary key and a primary key made of more than one column. The second is completely normal and is called a composite primary key: you list several columns in one `PRIMARY KEY` clause, and the database enforces uniqueness on the combination. This is the right design for junction tables, identified by the pair of foreign keys, and for weak entities like transaction line items identified by the pair of transaction id and line number.

When you need several columns to be independently unique, you add unique constraints, not more primary keys. A table can have one primary key plus as many unique constraints as needed. The senior nuance is that wide composite primary keys hurt performance because the PK is copied into every secondary index and every referencing foreign key, so many teams prefer a single narrow surrogate primary key and demote the natural combination to a unique constraint. At National Bank of India, transaction line items use a composite primary key on transaction id plus line number because a line has no identity outside its transaction.

Remember one sentence: exactly one primary key per table, but it may be composite, and any extra uniqueness comes from unique constraints, never from additional primary keys.
